docs.text:
type Skill struct {
    ID          string
    Name        string         // Lowercase slug, e.g. "deploy-checklist"
    Description string
    Content     string         // Full Markdown content
    Metadata    map[string]any
    ProjectID   *string        // nil = global
    CreatedAt   time.Time
    UpdatedAt   time.Time
}

docs.title: CreateSkillRequest
docs.text:
type CreateSkillRequest struct {
    Name        string         // Required. Lowercase slug, max 64 chars.
    Description string         // Required. Used for semantic retrieval.
    Content     string         // Required. Markdown workflow instructions.
    Metadata    map[string]any // Optional.
}

docs.title: UpdateSkillRequest
docs.text:
All fields are optional (pointer or omitempty). Only provided fields are updated.

type UpdateSkillRequest struct {
    Description *string
    Content     *string
    Metadata    map[string]any
}

docs.title: Accessing the client
docs.text:
skills.Client is available on the top-level SDK client:

client.Skills.List(ctx, projectID)
client.Skills.Create(ctx, projectID, req)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// Create a global skill
skill, err := client.Skills.Create(ctx, "", &skills.CreateSkillRequest{
    Name:        "deploy-checklist",
    Description: "Step-by-step deployment checklist for production releases",
    Content:     "# Deploy Checklist\n\n1. Run tests\n2. Tag the release\n3. Push to registry\n",
})
fmt.Printf("Created skill: %s (%s)\n", skill.Name, skill.ID)

// Create a project-scoped skill (overrides global for this project)
projectSkill, err := client.Skills.Create(ctx, projectID, &skills.CreateSkillRequest{
    Name:        "deploy-checklist",
    Description: "Custom deploy steps for this project",
    Content:     "# Project Deploy\n\n...",
})

// List merged skills for a project (global + project, project wins on conflict)
allSkills, err := client.Skills.List(ctx, projectID)
for _, s := range allSkills {
    scope := "global"
    if s.ProjectID != nil {
        scope = "project"
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s [%s] — %s\n", s.Name, scope, s.Description)
}

// Update description and content
updated, err := client.Skills.Update(ctx, skill.ID, &skills.UpdateSkillRequest{
    Description: strPtr("Updated description for better semantic retrieval"),
    Content:     strPtr("# Deploy Checklist v2\n\n..."),
})

// Delete
err = client.Skills.Delete(ctx, skill.ID)

docs.text:
// Verify superadmin role
me, err := client.Superadmin.GetMe(ctx)

    log.Fatal("not a superadmin")
}

// List failed extraction jobs platform-wide
hasErr := true
jobs, err := client.Superadmin.ListExtractionJobs(ctx, &superadmin.ListExtractionJobsOptions{
    HasError: &hasErr,
    Limit:    50,
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Printf("Failed extraction jobs: %d / %d total\n", jobs.Stats.Failed, jobs.Stats.Total)

// Cancel all queued jobs
var ids []string
for _, j := range jobs.Jobs {
    if j.Status == "queued" {
        ids = append(ids, j.ID)
    }
}
if len(ids) > 0 {
    result, err := client.Superadmin.CancelExtractionJobs(ctx, &superadmin.CancelJobsRequest{IDs: ids})
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("Cancelled %d jobs\n", result.CancelledCount)
}

Tasks are human-review items — such as AI-generated suggestions or flagged content — that require explicit acceptance, rejection, or cancellation. They are project-scoped and tied to a review/resolution workflow.

func AssertJSONBody(t *testing.T, r *http.Request, expected interface{})

These helpers call t.Fatal on mismatch, making test failures clear.

ms.On("POST", "/api/graph/objects", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    testutil.AssertMethod(t, r, "POST")
    testutil.AssertHeader(t, r, "X-Project-ID", "proj_123")
    testutil.AssertJSONBody(t, r, &graph.CreateObjectRequest{Type: "Note"})
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(testutil.FixtureGraphObject())
})

docs.title: useractivity
docs.text:
Package useractivity provides a client for the Memory User Activity API.

The user activity client tracks recently accessed resources per user — such as documents, graphs, and agents — enabling "recently viewed" UI features and navigation shortcuts.

docs.title: Import
docs.text: import "github.com/emergent-company/emergent.memory/apps/server/pkg/sdk/useractivity"

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
type Client struct { /* unexported */ }

Obtained via sdk.Client.UserActivity after calling client.SetContext(orgID, projectID).

docs.title: SetContext
docs.text:
func (c *Client) SetContext(orgID, projectID string)

Updates the X-Org-ID and X-Project-ID headers sent with every request. Thread-safe.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
func (c *Client) Record(ctx context.Context, projectID string, recordReq *RecordActivityRequest) error

Records a user activity event for a resource in a specific project. projectID is required and is passed as a query parameter (not a header).

Endpoint: POST /api/user-activity/record

docs.title: GetRecent
docs.text:
func (c *Client) GetRecent(ctx context.Context, opts *ListOptions) (*RecentItemsResponse, error)

Returns recently accessed resources across all resource types for the authenticated user, ordered most-recent first.

Endpoint: GET /api/user-activity/recent

docs.title: GetRecentByType
docs.text:
func (c *Client) GetRecentByType(ctx context.Context, resourceType string, opts *ListOptions) (*RecentItemsResponse, error)

Returns recently accessed resources filtered to a specific resourceType.

Endpoint: GET /api/user-activity/recent/{resourceType}

docs.title: DeleteAll
docs.text:
func (c *Client) DeleteAll(ctx context.Context) error

Clears all recent activity history for the authenticated user.

Endpoint: DELETE /api/user-activity/recent

docs.title: DeleteByResource
docs.text:
func (c *Client) DeleteByResource(ctx context.Context, resourceType, resourceID string) error

Removes a specific resource from the user's recent activity history.

Endpoint: DELETE /api/user-activity/recent/{resourceType}/{resourceID}

docs.title: RecentItem
docs.text:
type RecentItem struct {
    ID              string    `json:"id"`
    ResourceType    string    `json:"resourceType"`
    ResourceID      string    `json:"resourceId"`
    ResourceName    *string   `json:"resourceName,omitempty"`
    ResourceSubtype *string   `json:"resourceSubtype,omitempty"`
    ActionType      string    `json:"actionType"`
    AccessedAt      time.Time `json:"accessedAt"`
    ProjectID       string    `json:"projectId"`
}
Field Description ResourceType Type of resource, e.g., "document", "graph-object", "agent" ResourceID The ID of the accessed resource ResourceSubtype Optional sub-classification (e.g., object type) ActionType The action performed, e.g., "view", "edit" AccessedAt Timestamp of the access event

docs.title: RecentItemsResponse
docs.text:
type RecentItemsResponse struct {
    Data []RecentItem `json:"data"`
}

docs.title: RecordActivityRequest
docs.text:
type RecordActivityRequest struct {
    ResourceType    string  `json:"resourceType"`
    ResourceID      string  `json:"resourceId"`
    ResourceName    *string `json:"resourceName,omitempty"`
    ResourceSubtype *string `json:"resourceSubtype,omitempty"`
    ActionType      string  `json:"actionType"`
}

docs.title: ListOptions
docs.text:
type ListOptions struct {
    Limit int // Max results (default 20, max 100)
}

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
// Record a "view" event when the user opens a document
subtype := "pdf"
err := client.UserActivity.Record(ctx, projectID, &useractivity.RecordActivityRequest{
    ResourceType:    "document",
    ResourceID:      docID,
    ResourceName:    &docName,
    ResourceSubtype: &subtype,
    ActionType:      "view",
})
if err != nil {
    log.Printf("record activity: %v", err)
}

// Fetch the 10 most recently viewed documents
recent, err := client.UserActivity.GetRecentByType(ctx, "document", &useractivity.ListOptions{
    Limit: 10,
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, item := range recent.Data {
    fmt.Printf("%s — viewed %s\n", *item.ResourceName, item.AccessedAt.Format(time.RFC3339))
}

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: Memory is a graph-native AI knowledge platform. It lets you store, connect, and query information as a structured knowledge graph — then use AI to extract insights, answer questions, and automate workflows over that knowledge.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text: Capability Description Knowledge Graph Store typed objects and relationships, search semantically or by keyword Documents Upload files and URLs; the platform chunks and indexes them automatically Chat Ask questions about your knowledge graph in natural language Agents Automate workflows with AI agents that read and write the graph Blueprints Install schema packs, agents, skills, and seed data as one versioned bundle Branches Create isolated copies of the graph for safe editing and merging Data Sources Connect external systems (email, Google Drive, ClickUp) and sync automatically

docs.title: How it's organized
docs.text:
Organization
└── Project (your knowledge workspace)
    ├── Graph objects & relationships
    ├── Documents
    ├── Chat conversations
    ├── Agents
    └── Branches

Everything lives inside a project. A project belongs to an organization. You can be a member of multiple organizations and projects.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
• Getting Started

    Create your org, invite your team, set up your first project.

  • Knowledge Graph

    Add objects, define relationships, search and traverse the graph.

  • Documents

    Upload files and URLs to build your knowledge base.

  • Chat

    Ask questions and explore your knowledge graph via AI chat.

  • Agents

    Automate workflows with scheduled or event-driven AI agents.

  • Blueprints

    Install schema packs, agents, skills, and seed data as one versioned bundle.

  • Branches

    Work on isolated graph changes and merge them when ready.

  • Data Sources

    Connect and sync external data sources into your graph.

  • API Tokens

    Generate tokens for programmatic and CI/CD access.

  • Backups

    Create and restore project backups.

  • Notifications

    Stay informed about agent activity and system events.

  • Tasks

    Monitor and resolve background task operations.

  • Integrations

    Connect GitHub and other third-party services.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agents are AI workers that read and write your knowledge graph autonomously. You define what they do (system prompt, tools, model) and when they run (on demand, on a schedule, or in response to events).

Prerequisites: Agents require a generative model configured at the project or org level. If you haven't done that yet, see Model Setup first.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Concept Description Agent Definition Reusable blueprint: system prompt, model, tools Agent Runtime instance: trigger type, schedule, enabled state Agent Run One execution: status, steps, messages, tool calls

An Agent points to an Agent Definition. You trigger an Agent, which creates an Agent Run.

docs.title: Step 1 — Create an Agent Definition
docs.text:
The definition controls what the agent does.

memory defs create \
  --name "document-summarizer" \
  --system-prompt "You are an expert at summarizing technical documents. Extract key points and write a concise summary." \
  --model "gemini-2.0-flash" \
  --tools "search,graph_query,graph_create_object" \
  --visibility project \
  --max-steps 20
Flag Description --name Unique name within the project (required) --system-prompt Instructions for the LLM --model Model name, e.g. gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-2.5-flash --tools Comma-separated tool names the agent may call --visibility project (default), internal (system only), external (ACP-exposed) --max-steps Hard cap on LLM steps per run (default: 500)

To configure Google native tools or fine-tune temperature and token limits, use the Agent Definitions settings page in the Admin UI — see Google Native Tools below.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a Runtime Agent
docs.text:
The agent controls when the definition runs.

Manual (on demand)Scheduled (cron)Reaction (graph events)Webhook (external trigger) 
memory agents create \
  --name "doc-summarizer" \
  --trigger-type manual

memory agents create \
  --name "nightly-report" \
  --trigger-type schedule \
  --cron "0 2 * * *"

Cron format: minute hour dom month dow (standard 5-field).

The server also rejects a schedule that fires more often than every 15 minutes (its default safeguard).

memory agents create \
  --name "auto-tagger" \
  --trigger-type reaction \
  --reaction-events "created,updated" \
  --reaction-object-types "document"

memory agents create \
  --name "ci-trigger" \
  --trigger-type webhook

See Webhook Hooks below for the token setup.

docs.title: Step 3 — Trigger a Run
docs.text: memory agents trigger <agent-id>

docs.title: Step 4 — Monitor Runs
docs.text:
memory agents runs <agent-id> --limit 10

1. Run a1b2c3d4
   Status:    completed
   Started:   2026-03-08 14:22:01
   Completed: 2026-03-08 14:22:15
   Duration:  14230ms

2. Run e5f6g7h8
   Status:    failed
   Error:     max steps exceeded

Statuses: running · completed · failed · skipped · cancelled

docs.title: Human-in-the-Loop
docs.text: If the agent includes the ask_user tool, execution pauses when the agent calls it and waits for your response.

docs.title: See pending questions
docs.text: memory agents questions list-project --status pending

docs.title: Respond to resume execution
docs.text: memory agents questions respond <question-id> "My answer here"

docs.title: Webhook Hooks
docs.text: Webhooks let external systems (CI/CD, GitHub Actions) trigger an agent via HTTP.

docs.title: Create a hook
docs.text:
memory agents hooks create <agent-id> \
  --label "GitHub Actions" \
  --rate-limit 30 \
  --burst-size 5

Save the token

The plaintext bearer token is shown once only at creation time. Store it securely.

docs.title: Trigger from an external system
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/api/webhooks/agents/<hook-id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

docs.title: Manage hooks
docs.text:
memory agents hooks list <agent-id>
memory agents hooks delete <agent-id> <hook-id>

docs.title: Available Tools
docs.text:
Agents can be given access to tools from the following categories:

Category Tool names Knowledge graph graph_query, graph_create_object, graph_update_object, graph_search Search search Workspace (bash/file) workspace_bash, workspace_read, workspace_write, workspace_edit, workspace_glob, workspace_grep, workspace_git Human-in-the-loop ask_user Coordination spawn_agents, list_available_agents Skills skill

Specify tools as a comma-separated list in the agent definition. Glob patterns are supported (e.g. graph_*).

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Skills are reusable Markdown workflow instructions stored in the database. An agent with the skill tool can load any skill by name at runtime, keeping system prompts lean and instructions easy to update without redeploying agents.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At run start, the executor retrieves the skills available to the agent (global + project-scoped, with project skills winning on name collision).
  2. If the total skill count is ≤ 50, all skill names and descriptions are listed in the tool description. If > 50, the executor embeds the agent's trigger message and surfaces the top-10 semantically relevant skills.
  3. The agent calls skill({name: "..."}) to load a skill's full Markdown content.

docs.title: Opt in via the agent definition
docs.text:
Add "skill" to the agent's tools list:

memory defs create \
  --name "onboarding-agent" \
  --system-prompt "You onboard new team members. Use the skill tool to load relevant playbooks." \
  --model "gemini-2.0-flash" \
  --tools "skill,graph_query,graph_create_object"

Or update an existing definition:

memory defs update <definition-id> --tools "skill,search,graph_query"

docs.title: Manage skills via the CLI
docs.text:
Skills use a lowercase slug name (e.g. my-skill, max 64 characters). Letters, digits and single hyphens or dots are allowed; dots are reserved for learned skills (see below).

List skills

memory skills list                        # global skills
memory skills list --project <project-id> # global + project-scoped, merged

Create a skill

memory skills create \
  --name "deploy-checklist" \
  --description "Step-by-step deployment checklist for production releases" \
  --content-file ./deploy-checklist.md

# Project-scoped (overrides a global skill with the same name within this project)
memory skills create \
  --name "deploy-checklist" \
  --description "Custom deploy steps for this project" \
  --content-file ./my-deploy.md \
  --project <project-id>

Import from a SKILL.md file (YAML frontmatter format)

memory skills import ./path/to/SKILL.md
memory skills import ./path/to/SKILL.md --project <project-id>

The file must have name and description in YAML frontmatter:

---
name: deploy-checklist
description: Step-by-step deployment checklist for production releases
---
# Deploy Checklist

1. Run tests
2. Tag the release
...

Get, update, delete

memory skills get <id>
memory skills update <id> --description "Updated description"
memory skills update <id> --content-file ./new-content.md
memory skills delete <id>
memory skills delete <id> --confirm   # skip confirmation prompt

docs.title: Scope and visibility
docs.text:
Scope Created via Visible to Global POST /api/skills (no project) All agents in all projects Project-scoped POST /api/projects/:id/skills Agents in that project only

When a project-scoped skill has the same name as a global skill, the project-scoped version takes precedence for agents in that project.

docs.title: Seed from existing SKILL.md files
docs.text:
If you have existing .agents/skills/*/SKILL.md files following the OpenCode format, import them all at once:

for f in .agents/skills/*/SKILL.md; do
  memory skills import "$f"
done

docs.title: Automatic skill capture (opt-in)
docs.text:
An agent can learn from its own successful runs: a bounded background review turns a run into a staged proposal, and a human decides whether it becomes a skill. The feature is off everywhere until a project opts in.

Enable it on a project

Open Settings → General → Skill capture and pick a mode (off, suggest, or auto). The Auto-apply captured skills toggle sits below it and is only enabled in auto. Or PATCH the project:

curl -X PATCH "$MEMORY_API/api/projects/$PROJECT_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"skill_capture": {"mode": "suggest"}}'

mode is off (default), suggest, or auto. suggest is the recommended starting point: every candidate waits for approval. auto additionally requires auto-apply to be on (the toggle above, or "autoApply": true in the API), and passes only when the candidate is clean, confident, not a duplicate, not a delete, within the daily caps, and the agent has at least one previously approved proposal. Deletes are always human-reviewed.

Narrow it per agent

Each agent's Settings → Skills page has an Automatic skill capture control: Inherit project setting, Suggest only, or Off. The same override is available as skillCapture: {"mode": "off"} on the agent definition. It can only narrow the project policy — it never widens it, so the project mode stays the master switch. An override that is not set inherits the project value.

What the agent writes. Learned skills are named {agent-slug}.{topic} (for example research-assistant.handling-empty-results) and are auto-loaded on the next run when the agent has autoLoadSkills enabled. Skills the agent writes are marked as agent-created; the scheduled curator ages them active → stale → archived when unused. Pin a skill to stop ageing, or lock it to refuse further agent writes.

Archived skills stay in the Agents → Skills list, marked with an Archived badge, but are no longer loaded or retrieved by agents. Use Restore or Restore & pin on that row (or open the skill first) to return it to active; Restore & pin also pins it so the curator never ages it out again. Restoring preserves every other metadata field. The same action is available over the API:

POST /api/projects/:projectId/skills/:id/restore   # optional body: {"pin": true}

Review the inbox

Open Agents → Skills. A Proposed skills panel sits above the skill list and shows every pending proposal: the skill name, the agent it came from, the change kind (create, patch or delete), the capture confidence, and the current linter and security findings. Approve applies the proposal; Reject discards it. Both actions return to the same panel, and a failed approve — the security scan runs again and can still block the write — leaves the proposal pending and shows the error. Approved and rejected proposals drop out of the panel; it lists pending decisions only.

The same inbox is available over the API:

GET  /api/projects/:projectId/skills/proposals              # pending by default
GET  /api/projects/:projectId/skills/proposals/:proposalId
POST /api/projects/:projectId/skills/proposals/:proposalId/approve
POST /api/projects/:projectId/skills/proposals/:proposalId/reject

Approving applies the proposal through the normal skill write path, so content hashes, embeddings and provenance stay consistent. The security scan runs again at approval.

Operators can stop the whole loop without a migration by setting MEMORY_SKILL_CAPTURE_DISABLED=1.

docs.title: Google Native Tools
docs.text:
Gemini models expose a set of built-in tools that are invoked directly by the model — no function-calling round-trip required. You opt into them per agent definition.

Tool What it does Minimum model google_search Live web search via Google Gemini 2.0 Flash code_execution Runs Python in a sandboxed environment; output is returned to the model Gemini 2.0 Flash url_context Fetches and reads the content of URLs mentioned in the conversation Gemini 2.5 Flash

Gemini only

Native tools are only available on Gemini models (Google AI or Vertex AI). They are silently ignored when the agent is configured with a non-Gemini model.

Model capability check

If a tool is requested but the selected model does not support it, it is silently skipped at runtime. For example, requesting url_context on gemini-2.0-flash has no effect.

docs.title: Configure via the Admin UI
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Project → Agent Definitions.
  2. Click New Definition or edit an existing one.
  3. Under Model Configuration, enter a Gemini model name (e.g. gemini-2.5-flash-preview-0514).
  4. Check the native tools you want to enable.
  5. Click Save Definition.

docs.title: Configure via the API
docs.text:
Include nativeTools in the model object when creating or updating a definition:

{
  "name": "web-researcher",
  "systemPrompt": "You are a research assistant. Use web search to find current information.",
  "model": {
    "name": "gemini-2.5-flash-preview-0514",
    "temperature": 1.0,
    "nativeTools": ["google_search", "url_context"]
  }
}

PATCH /api/projects/{projectId}/agent-definitions/{id} accepts the same shape.

docs.title: Configure via Blueprints
docs.text:
# agents/web-researcher.yaml
name: web-researcher
systemPrompt: |
  You are a research assistant. Use web search to find current information.
model:
  name: gemini-2.5-flash-preview-0514
  temperature: 1.0
  nativeTools:
    - google_search
    - url_context
tools:
  - graph_create_object
  - graph_query
visibility: project

docs.title: Model support matrix
docs.text:
Model google_search url_context code_execution gemini-2.5-pro-* ✓ ✓ ✓ gemini-2.5-flash-* ✓ ✓ ✓ gemini-2.5-flash-lite-* ✓ ✓ ✓ gemini-2.0-flash-* ✓ — ✓ gemini-2.0-flash-lite-* — — — gemini-3-flash-* ✓ ✓ ✓ gemini-3-pro-* ✓ ✓ ✓

url_context was introduced in the Gemini 2.5 generation. Image generation variants (*-image-preview) support google_search only.

docs.title: Blueprints (GitOps)
docs.text:
Define agent definitions as YAML and apply them repeatably. Blueprints can also carry schema packs, skills, and seed data — see Blueprints.

# agents/document-summarizer.yaml
name: document-summarizer
systemPrompt: |
  You are an expert at summarizing technical documents.
model:
  name: gemini-2.0-flash
  temperature: 0.7
  maxSteps: 20
tools:
  - search
  - graph_query
visibility: project

memory blueprints install ./my-blueprints --project my-project
memory blueprints install ./my-blueprints --dry-run   # preview only
memory blueprints install ./my-blueprints --upgrade   # update existing

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# Definitions
memory defs list
memory defs create --name <n> --system-prompt <p> --model <m> --tools <t1,t2>
memory defs update <id> [flags]
memory defs delete <id>

# Agents
memory agents list
memory agents create --name <n> --trigger-type manual|schedule|reaction|webhook
memory agents trigger <id>
memory agents runs <id> [--limit <n>]
memory agents update <id> [flags]
memory agents delete <id>

# Human-in-the-loop
memory agents questions list-project [--status pending]
memory agents questions respond <question-id> "<answer>"

# Webhook hooks
memory agents hooks list <agent-id>
memory agents hooks create <agent-id> --label <l>
memory agents hooks delete <agent-id> <hook-id>

# Skills
memory skills list [--project <id>] [--global]
memory skills get <id>
memory skills create --name <n> --description <d> --content-file <path> [--project <id>]
memory skills update <id> [--description <d>] [--content-file <path>]
memory skills delete <id> [--confirm]
memory skills import <path/to/SKILL.md> [--project <id>]

docs.title: Safety Limits
docs.text: Limit Default Max steps per run 500 (configurable via --max-steps) Doom loop detection Halts after 5 consecutive identical tool calls Webhook rate limiting Configurable per hook via --rate-limit (req/min)

docs.title: API Tokens
docs.text: API tokens let scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and third-party tools authenticate to Memory without an interactive login. Tokens are scoped to a project and carry only the permissions you grant.

docs.title: Token format
docs.text:
All tokens use the prefix emt_ (e.g. emt_abc123...). Tokens are:

  • Scoped to a specific project
  • Revocable at any time
  • Auditable — lastUsedAt tracks recent activity
  • Stored as a bcrypt hash — the plaintext value is only shown at creation

docs.title: Creating a Token
docs.text:
CLIAPI 
memory tokens create \
  --name "CI/CD Pipeline" \
  --scopes "documents:read,search,agents:write" \
  --project my-project

The CLI also accepts presets: --scopes read (the read-only set), --scopes write (the write set, which also implies the matching reads) or --scopes read,write for both.

POST /api/projects/{projectId}/tokens
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "CI/CD Pipeline",
  "scopes": ["documents:read", "search", "agents:write"]
}

Response (token value shown once only): 

{
  "id": "tok_abc123",
  "name": "CI/CD Pipeline",
  "token": "emt_abc123...",
  "scopes": ["documents:read", "search", "agents:write"],
  "tokenPrefix": "emt_abc",
  "createdAt": "2026-03-08T10:00:00Z"
}

Save the token value

The full token is returned only at creation. It cannot be retrieved again. Store it in a secrets manager (GitHub Secrets, Vault, etc.) immediately.

docs.title: Scopes Reference
docs.text:
Scope Access documents:read Read documents documents:write Create and update documents documents:delete Delete documents ingest:write Trigger document ingestion/parsing chunks:read Read document chunks chunks:write Create and update chunks graph:read Read graph objects graph:write Create and update graph objects graph:search:read Graph vector search search Run hybrid and semantic search (MCP) search:read Unified REST search journal:read Read the project journal extraction:read View extraction jobs extraction:write Manage extraction jobs tasks:read Read tasks tasks:write Resolve and cancel tasks notifications:read Read notifications notifications:write Mark notifications as read user-activity:read View the activity log user-activity:write Write activity entries schema:read Read type definitions and template packs schema:write Install and modify schemas agents:read Read agents, runs, definitions, questions agents:write Trigger agents, respond to questions, manage hooks projects:read Read project metadata and members projects:write Update project settings and members

Assign only the scopes your integration needs. The full list, including branch, skill and admin scopes, is in Security and Scopes.

The CLI also accepts two presets: --scopes read (the read-only set above) and --scopes write (documents, graph, schema, agents and project writes, plus the REST write scopes the retired data:write umbrella used to imply). Combine them with --scopes read,write.

data:read and data:write are retired

The coarse data:read / data:write umbrellas can no longer be requested when creating or editing a token — the CLI, web UI, API and connectors all reject them. Use the fine-grained scopes above instead. Tokens minted before the change keep exactly the access they had; a token that still holds one cannot be re-scoped in the web UI, so create a replacement and revoke it (or update its scopes through the API, which accepts a set that drops the umbrella).

Every fine-grained scope the umbrellas implied is mintable, so a replacement token can request the exact REST scopes it needs. See Security and Scopes.

docs.title: Using a Token
Listing Tokens
docs.text:
memory tokens list --project my-project

GET /api/projects/{projectId}/tokens

Response shows token metadata but never the plaintext value. Use tokenPrefix to identify which token is which.

docs.title: Revoking a Token
docs.text:
memory tokens revoke <token-id> --project my-project

DELETE /api/projects/{projectId}/tokens/{tokenId}

The token is invalidated immediately. Any requests using it will receive 401 Unauthorized.

docs.title: CI/CD Example
docs.text:
# GitHub Actions
- name: Trigger nightly agent
  run: |
    memory agents trigger $AGENT_ID --project $PROJECT_ID
  env:
    MEMORY_SERVER_URL: https://api.example.com
    MEMORY_PROJECT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MEMORY_TOKEN }}

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Memory supports project-level backups. A backup captures the complete state of a project — graph objects, relationships, documents, and metadata — and stores it for later restoration.

docs.title: Creating a Backup
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/backups
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "backupType": "full"
}

Backup creation is asynchronous. The response returns a backup record with status: "creating". Poll to check progress.

docs.title: Backup types
docs.text: Type Description full Complete snapshot of all project data incremental Only the changes since the last backup (parentBackupId required)

docs.title: Scheduled backups
docs.text:
A project can run its backups automatically. Each project has at most one schedule: enable it, set a cadence, and the server starts a normal backup every time the cadence fires.

PUT /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/backup-schedule
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "enabled": true,
  "cronSchedule": "0 2 * * *",
  "retentionDays": 30,
  "includeChat": false,
  "includeJournal": false,
  "includeDeleted": false
}
Field Description enabled Whether the schedule runs. Defaults to true when omitted on save. cronSchedule Standard 5-field cron (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week) evaluated in UTC. retentionDays Retention applied to every backup the schedule creates. Default 30, range 1–365. includeChat / includeJournal / includeDeleted What each scheduled archive includes.

Reading, and removing, the schedule:

GET    /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/backup-schedule   # 404 when no schedule is configured
DELETE /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/backup-schedule   # 204

Rules:

  • Minimum interval is 15 minutes. A cron expression that fires more often is rejected with 400. Common cadences: 0 * * * * (hourly), 0 */6 * * * (every 6 hours), 0 2 * * * (daily 02:00 UTC), 0 2 * * 0 (weekly, Sunday).
  • Schedules are evaluated in UTC, so they do not follow the viewer's timezone or daylight-saving shifts.
  • Editing recomputes the next run immediately — a new cadence applies at once instead of waiting out the old expression.
  • Missed fires collapse into one catch-up run. If the server was down across several slots, the schedule runs once and then resumes at the next slot rather than firing a burst.
  • No pile-up. A due fire is skipped when the project already has a backup in progress (status: "creating").
  • Scheduled backups are attributed to the user who saved the schedule, and the lastBackupId on the schedule points at the most recent one.

The schedule's response also carries the runner's bookkeeping:

Field Description nextRunAt Next time the schedule will fire (UTC) lastRunAt When a fire last started a backup (a fire skipped by the pile-up guard does not move it) lastBackupId The backup the last fire started

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
expiresAt is written at creation (createdAt + retentionDays, default 30 days). A daily sweep enforces it:

  1. A backup whose expiresAt has passed is soft-deleted — it disappears from the backups list but its row and archive are kept.
  2. After a 14-day grace window, the archive object and row are purged.

The grace window is deliberate: an over-aggressive retentionDays costs a support request, not the data.

docs.title: Managing schedules from the CLI
docs.text:
memory backups schedule set --cron "0 2 * * *"                 # create or replace
memory backups schedule set --cron "0 */6 * * *" --retention-days 14 --include-chat
memory backups schedule set --cron "0 2 * * *" --disabled      # save, but do not run
memory backups schedule get                                     # "No backup schedule configured." when unset
memory backups schedule delete

The same controls are on the Backups page in the web UI, in the Scheduled backups card.

docs.title: Backup status fields
docs.text: Field Description status creating · ready · failed · deleted progress Integer 0–100 indicating completion percentage sizeBytes Size of the backup archive in bytes errorMessage Present if status is failed completedAt Timestamp when the backup finished expiresAt Expiry after which the backup is auto-deleted (set from the create request's retentionDays, default 30 days) stats Object counts and other summary metrics

docs.title: Listing Backups
docs.text: GET /api/v1/organizations/{orgId}/backups

docs.title: Getting a Backup
docs.text: GET /api/v1/organizations/{orgId}/backups/{backupId}

docs.title: Downloading a Backup
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/organizations/{orgId}/backups/{backupId}/download

Returns a signed download URL or streams the backup archive directly.

docs.title: Restoring a Backup
docs.text:
Destructive operation

Restoring a backup overwrites the current project state. This cannot be undone. Create a fresh backup before restoring if you want to preserve the current state.

POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/restore
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "backupId": "<backup-id>"
}

Monitor the restore job:

GET /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/restores/{restoreId}

docs.title: Deleting a Backup
docs.text: DELETE /api/v1/organizations/{orgId}/backups/{backupId}

docs.title: Importing an archive from another deployment
docs.text:
Backups are self-describing ZIP archives (manifest.json, project/config.json, database/*.ndjson, files/*). You can import an archive produced by another deployment so it can be restored locally.

POST /api/v1/organizations/{orgId}/backups/import
Content-Type: multipart/form-data

file: <backup.zip>
retentionDays: 30   # optional, 1-365 (default 30)

Requirements and limits:

Constraint Value Field file (multipart/form-data) Maximum size 1 GiB Format ZIP only Authorization Must be a member of the target organization Manifest Must pass structure, project-id, and checksum validation

On success the endpoint returns 201 Created with a backup record that has status: "ready" and imported: true. Its projectId records the archive's source project — a foreign project that does not exist in this deployment.

Imported backups are clone-only. They cannot be used for an overwrite restore (overwrite requires a local project matching the source project id). To restore an imported backup, clone it into the target organization:

POST /api/v1/organizations/{orgId}/restore
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "backupId": "<imported-backup-id>",
  "targetProjectName": "Restored project"
}

The clone creates a new project with a new project id, drops foreign user references, and adds the restoring user to the new project.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text: Each backup includes manifestChecksum and contentChecksum for integrity verification. Compare these values after downloading to confirm the archive has not been corrupted.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
A blueprint is a versioned, declarative bundle that a project can apply as a unit: schema packs, agent definitions, skills, and seed graph objects and relationships. Applying a blueprint materializes its content into the project; un-applying removes only the content that blueprint owned.

Blueprints are how a project gets a working domain model without hand-building every type, agent, and seed row. They are also the recommended way to share a setup across projects or teams.

docs.title: What a blueprint contains
docs.text:
Part What it does Apply semantics Schema packs (packs) Object types and relationship types Created if absent; always assigned to the applying project Agent definitions (agents) Runtime agents (prompt, model, tools) Create-or-update by name Skills (skills) Markdown skill files (agentskills.io format) Create-or-update by name, global scope Seed (seed) Graph objects and relationships Idempotent — keyed objects upsert; objects without a key are skipped

A blueprint may carry any subset. Of the built-ins, operator ships only an agent definition and agent-notes/dreaming-agent/session-message-types ship only a schema pack; the example code-memory-blueprint in the product repo's blueprints/ directory is schema-only too.

docs.title: Where blueprints come from
docs.text:
Every blueprint lives in a registry and has an origin:

Origin Scope Who can change it builtin Global (visible to every project) Nobody — immutable, fork it user Private to the project that created it The owning project import Private to the project, imported from a GitHub repo The owning project

Global built-in blueprints are seeded at server startup and are readable and apply-able by every project, but never editable. To change one, fork it with blueprint-new-version and edit your own copy.

docs.title: Built-in blueprints
docs.text:
Blueprint What it installs task-board Board-enabled Task object type, a reaction-triggered task-worker agent with its task-workflow skill, one example seed task agent-notes The agent-notes schema pack only (no agent definition) dreaming-agent The dreaming-agent schema pack only — the Dream object type and its relationships, no agent definition operator One general-assistant agent that can read and change platform settings (every change proposed, then applied on acceptance) session-message-types The session-message-types schema pack (object types for chat session messages)

More example blueprints live in the product repository under blueprints/ and install as GitHub imports (multi-agent, code-memory-blueprint, blueprint-architect, security-review, webpage-feedback, …).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
create / import  ──▶  draft  ──publish──▶  published  ──apply──▶  applied
                          ▲                    │                     │
                          └── new-version ─────┘                 unapply
                                                                     │
                                                                  unapplied
  • Draft — editable. Description, author, and manifest can change.
  • Publish — computes a sha256 checksum over the manifest and freezes the version. A published blueprint is immutable; edits need a new version.
  • Apply — materializes the manifest into the calling project and records the application as provenance for everything it created.
  • Unapply — reverses that application (see Un-applying).
  • Deprecate — marks a published blueprint as deprecated. It stays readable, but it can no longer be applied: apply rejects anything that is not draft or published. It is a signal, not a removal.
  • Delete — only for user/import blueprints, and only while unapplied. Built-ins cannot be deleted.

Versions are addressed by (name, version). blueprint-versions (or GET /api/blueprints/name/:name/versions) lists every version you can see, newest first; blueprint-new-version clones any readable blueprint — including a built-in — into a draft in your project, where you can edit and publish it.

docs.title: With MCP
docs.text:
// blueprint-create
{
  "name": "crm",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Sales pipeline over the knowledge graph",
  "manifest": {
    "packs": [ /* see the manifest shape below */ ],
    "agents": [],
    "skills": [],
    "seed": { "objects": [], "relationships": [] }
  }
}

blueprint-create returns the draft. Edit it with blueprint-update, freeze it with blueprint-publish, then blueprint-apply.

docs.title: Manifest shape
docs.text:
The manifest is the same document a CLI blueprint directory describes. Both camelCase and snake_case spellings of objectTypes/relationshipTypes (objectTypeSchemas/relationshipTypeSchemas) decode the same way:

name: crm
version: "1.0.0"
description: Sales pipeline over the knowledge graph
author: platform-team

packs:
  - name: crm
    version: "1.0.0"
    description: Companies, contacts, and deals
    objectTypes:
      - name: Company
        label: Company
        properties:
          name: { type: string, title: Company name }
          homepage: { type: url, title: Homepage }
      - name: Deal
        label: Deal
        properties:
          amount: { type: number, title: Amount }
    relationshipTypes:
      - name: works_at
        label: Works At
        sourceType: Contact
        targetType: Company

agents:
  - name: deal-desk
    systemPrompt: |
      Answer questions about the sales pipeline.
    model: { name: gemini-2.5-flash }

skills: []

seed:
  objects:
    - type: Company
      key: acme
      properties: { name: Acme Corp }
  relationships:
    - type: works_at
      srcKey: alice
      dstKey: acme

Property title is the label the UI shows (the key stays visible beneath it); url, sha256, and date are validated property types. See Schema § Property definitions for the full vocabulary.

docs.title: With the CLI (a directory)
docs.text:
The CLI applies a directory (or GitHub repo) directly — it does not go through the registry, so there is no draft/publish step:

memory blueprints inspect ./my-blueprint     # list contents, no API calls
memory blueprints validate ./my-blueprint    # offline, no API calls
memory blueprints install ./my-blueprint --dry-run
memory blueprints install ./my-blueprint --project my-project

Directory layout:

my-blueprint/
  schemas/                        # preferred; packs/ is accepted for compatibility
    crm.yaml
  agents/
    deal-desk.yaml
  skills/
    deal-review/SKILL.md          # agentskills.io: frontmatter + Markdown body
  seed/
    objects/Company.jsonl
    relationships/works_at.jsonl

To get a registry blueprint from a directory, import it as a GitHub repo (see GitHub import) — or create the draft over MCP/API and pass the same manifest.

docs.title: Applying a blueprint
docs.text:
MCPRESTWeb UI 
// blueprint-apply
{ "id": "<blueprint-uuid>" }

curl -X POST https://api.example.com/api/blueprints/<id>/apply \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "X-Project-ID: <projectId>"

Open Blueprints, choose a blueprint, and select Install.

Apply is not atomic: packs, agents, and skills fail fast and seed data is best-effort (counted in the result). Every step is idempotent, so a failed apply can be retried after fixing the manifest and will converge — the application (provenance) is recorded only after all steps succeed.

Built-in packs are shared: every project that applies the same built-in blueprint is assigned the same global source=builtin pack. user and import blueprints materialize project-scoped packs instead. Re-applying a built-in blueprint refreshes the pack definitions from the manifest, even under an unchanged (name, version), so a content fix reaches projects without a version bump.

docs.title: Model mapping
docs.text:
Blueprint agents pin a model. At install time you can map them to a model your project actually has configured:

memory blueprints install ./my-blueprint --map-model deal-desk=google/gemini-2.5-pro
memory blueprints install ./my-blueprint --map-model deal-desk=    # project default
memory blueprints install ./my-blueprint --no-map                  # keep pinned models

Overrides are persisted per project and keyed by blueprint name (GET/PUT /api/blueprints/model-overrides), and are applied before materialization — precedence: explicit request > stored override > manifest.

docs.title: Un-applying
docs.text:
blueprint-unapply (or POST /api/blueprints/:id/unapply) removes what the blueprint owned:

Content On unapply Agent definitions Deleted, scoped by source_blueprint_id Pack assignments Soft-deleted if this blueprint owns them Global pack row Kept — shared with other projects Skills Left in place (global scope) Seed objects/relationships Left in place (shared data, not owned)

An assignment is only removed when no other applied blueprint still claims the pack. Applying a newer version of the same blueprint re-points the assignment to the newer version; it never steals an assignment owned by a different blueprint name.

docs.title: Importing from GitHub
docs.text:
# Preview what the repo contains — creates nothing
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/api/blueprints/import/preview \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "X-Project-ID: <projectId>" \
  -d '{"url":"https://github.com/acme/memory-blueprints"}'

# Import (and optionally publish + apply)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/api/blueprints/import \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "X-Project-ID: <projectId>" \
  -d '{"url":"https://github.com/acme/memory-blueprints","ref":"v1.2.0","publish":true,"apply":true}'
  • Private repositories: store a project-scoped token with memory blueprints github-token set (encrypted at rest; never echoed back).
  • Re-importing an existing (name, version) adopts that row — refreshing a draft, reusing a published version — instead of failing with a conflict.
  • The server records the repo URL and ref as provenance and checks for upstream updates on a schedule.

docs.title: Checking for updates
docs.text:
memory blueprints check-updates            # status of every applied blueprint
memory blueprints check-updates crm        # trigger a check and print the result
memory blueprints update crm --wait        # apply the available update

Equivalent REST: GET /api/blueprints/:name/updates, POST /api/blueprints/:name/updates/check, POST /api/blueprints/:name/updates/apply.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
All blueprint commands resolve the project like the rest of the CLI (--project, or MEMORY_PROJECT / MEMORY_PROJECT_ID from .env.local).

Command Purpose memory blueprints install <source> Apply a directory or GitHub repo memory blueprints inspect <source> List contents without installing memory blueprints validate <source> Offline structural + cross-reference validation memory blueprints dump <dir> Export a project's objects/relationships as JSONL seed files memory blueprints check-updates [name] Check GitHub-imported blueprints for newer upstream versions memory blueprints update <name> Apply an available update memory blueprints github-token set Store the project's GitHub PAT for private repos

docs.title: install flags
docs.text: Flag Description --project <id> Target project ID or name --upgrade Update existing resources instead of skipping them --dry-run Preview actions without writing anything (it still reads project context) --token <tok> GitHub PAT for private repos (also MEMORY_GITHUB_TOKEN) --map-model agent=provider/model Map a blueprint agent to a project model (repeatable) --no-map Skip install-time model mapping; keep the blueprint's pinned models

docs.title: dump flags
docs.text:
Flag Description --project <id> Source project ID or name --types <list> Comma-separated object/relationship type filter (default: all)

validate exits 0 on clean or warnings-only, 1 on any error, and is fully offline — always run it before install. dump exports graph data only; it does not export packs or agent definitions.

docs.title: Importing a dump into a branch
docs.text:
dump writes seed/objects/<Type>.jsonl and seed/relationships/<Type>.jsonl with object keys and srcKey/dstKey references. To review a migration on a branch before promoting it, feed the dump directory straight back to the graph importer:

memory blueprints dump ./migration
# edit ./migration/seed/...
memory graph objects create-batch --file ./migration --branch migration-review

The importer upserts objects by key, resolves relationship keys after the objects are written, reads _untyped.jsonl back as type Untyped, and reports unreadable rows individually without aborting the rest. It accepts the dump root, a seed/ directory, or a single .jsonl file. See Branches § Bulk importing a dump into a branch.

docs.title: Registry commands (MCP and REST)
docs.text: The registry lifecycle — browse, draft, publish, version, apply, unapply, delete — is available over MCP and the REST API. The CLI covers the directory workflow and update checks, not registry browse/apply.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
Tool Scope Purpose blueprint-list schema:read Global built-ins plus your own private blueprints blueprint-get schema:read One blueprint, including its manifest blueprint-versions schema:read Every version of a name, newest first blueprint-list-applied schema:read Blueprints currently applied to the project blueprint-create schema:write Create a draft (project-private) blueprint-update schema:write Edit a draft's description, author, manifest blueprint-publish schema:write Freeze a draft, computing its checksum blueprint-new-version schema:write Fork any readable blueprint into a new draft blueprint-apply schema:write Materialize a blueprint into the project blueprint-unapply schema:write Reverse a previous apply

Creating a global blueprint (project_id NULL) requires superadmin_full; project members can author project-private drafts.

The REST API also exposes DELETE /api/blueprints/:id (delete an unapplied user/import blueprint) and POST /api/blueprints/:id/deprecate, plus the GitHub import, update-check, model-override, and GitHub-token endpoints. Those have no MCP tool equivalent yet.

docs.title: REST endpoints
docs.text: Method Path Purpose GET /api/blueprints List visible blueprints (optional ?name=) POST /api/blueprints Create a draft GET /api/blueprints/:id Get one blueprint PUT /api/blueprints/:id Update a draft DELETE /api/blueprints/:id Delete an unapplied user/import blueprint POST /api/blueprints/:id/publish Publish a draft POST /api/blueprints/:id/deprecate Mark published as deprecated POST /api/blueprints/:id/versions Fork into a new draft version GET /api/blueprints/name/:name/versions Versions by name POST /api/blueprints/:id/apply Apply to the project POST /api/blueprints/:id/unapply Unapply from the project GET /api/blueprints/applied Applied blueprints POST /api/blueprints/import Import from a GitHub repo POST /api/blueprints/import/preview Preview an import GET /api/blueprints/:name/updates Update status POST /api/blueprints/:name/updates/check Check upstream POST /api/blueprints/:name/updates/apply Apply the upstream update GET/PUT /api/blueprints/model-overrides Per-project agent model mapping PUT /api/blueprints/github-credentials Store the project's GitHub PAT

docs.title: Schema packs and provenance
docs.text:
Applying a blueprint is what makes a schema pack active in a project. The Schema area's Schema packs page (/schema/packs) lists each active pack with its types, an owner badge (Global for a shared built-in pack, Project for a project-owned one), and the applied blueprint that claims it.

For a given project, GET /api/schemas/projects/:projectId/pack-claims returns the packs claimed by at least one applied blueprint. Unapplied and superseded blueprints are omitted.

See Schema § Schema packs for the pack view and Schema Registry for the type-level model.

docs.title: Notes and gotchas
docs.text:
• Packs are always assigned on apply, even when the pack row already existed. That is what registers the types in the target project.
  • Set a key on every seed object. In the registry apply path (MCP, web UI, import-and-apply) an object with no key is skipped with a warning — keyless duplicates on re-apply are worse than a skip. The CLI's directory install is the opposite: it creates keyless objects on every run, so a re-install duplicates them.
  • Use srcKey/dstKey in relationships, not raw entity IDs — IDs do not survive an apply into another project.
  • Published means immutable. Correcting a published version requires new-version; re-publishing is refused.
  • Unapply is scoped. Skills and seed data stay; only agents and pack assignments owned by that blueprint are removed.
  • Global writes need superadmin_full. Project members can only create project-private (user) blueprints.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
Branches let you work on isolated copies of the knowledge graph — making changes, reviewing them, and merging back — without affecting the main graph until you're ready.

Think of it like git branches, but for your knowledge graph.

docs.title: When to use branches
docs.text:
• Reviewing AI-extracted content before it enters the main graph
  • Exploratory work — adding objects and relationships you may want to roll back
  • Parallel editing — multiple people working on separate sets of changes
  • Staged imports — loading a new data source into a branch, validating, then merging

docs.title: Creating a Branch
docs.text:
API 
POST /api/graph/branches
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "q4-planning-review",
  "project_id": "proj_xyz789"
}

Response: 

{
  "id": "branch_abc123",
  "name": "q4-planning-review",
  "project_id": "proj_xyz789",
  "parent_branch_id": null,
  "created_at": "2026-03-08T10:00:00Z"
}

docs.title: Branch from an existing branch
docs.text:
POST /api/graph/branches
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "sub-feature",
  "project_id": "proj_xyz789",
  "parent_branch_id": "branch_abc123"
}

docs.title: Working on a Branch
docs.text:
Pass branch_id in the request body when creating objects or relationships on a branch:

POST /api/graph/objects
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "type": "Decision",
  "branch_id": "branch_abc123",
  "properties": { "title": "Adopt event sourcing" }
}

For list/get requests, pass branch_id as a query parameter:

GET /api/graph/objects?branch_id=branch_abc123

Objects created on a branch are isolated — they are not visible in the main graph until you merge.

docs.title: Bulk importing a dump into a branch
docs.text:
memory blueprints dump <dir> exports the graph as JSONL seed files (seed/objects/<Type>.jsonl and seed/relationships/<Type>.jsonl). To stage a migration on a branch, edit the dump and import it in one call:

memory blueprints dump ./migration
# review/edit ./migration/seed/objects/*.jsonl and seed/relationships/*.jsonl
memory graph objects create-batch --file ./migration --branch migration-review

The importer:

  • accepts a dump root, a seed/ directory, or a single .jsonl file;
  • upserts objects by key (so re-running is safe) and reads _untyped.jsonl back as type Untyped;
  • resolves relationship srcKey/dstKey after the objects are written;
  • reports each unreadable row (bad JSON, missing type, unresolved key, server rejection) and continues, then exits non-zero if anything failed.

Everything lands on the named branch; the main graph is untouched until you merge.

Both batch commands take the same flag:

# objects (and optionally relationships) from a JSON/subgraph file
memory graph objects create-batch --file subgraph.json --branch migration-review

# relationships only, by existing entity IDs
memory graph relationships create-batch --file edges.json --branch migration-review

For relationships create-batch, both endpoint objects must already exist on the same branch — the server rejects a cross-branch edge.

docs.title: Listing Branches
docs.text: GET /api/graph/branches

docs.title: Getting a Branch
docs.text: GET /api/graph/branches/{id}

docs.title: Merging a Branch
docs.text:
When you are ready to promote changes from a source branch into a target branch, merge it.

Direction: source → target. The source branch is read; the target branch receives the changes.

By default the merge is a dry run — it shows what would change without mutating state. Pass "execute": true to apply.

POST /api/graph/branches/main/merge
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "source_branch_id": "branch_abc123"
}

Use main as the path segment to merge into the main graph. Use a branch UUID to merge into another branch.

Dry-run response shows each object classified as:

Classification Meaning added Exists on source only — will be created on target fast_forward Changed on source only — target will be updated conflict Changed on both branches — blocks execute until resolved unchanged Identical on both branches — nothing to do

To execute after reviewing:

POST /api/graph/branches/main/merge
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "source_branch_id": "branch_abc123",
  "execute": true
}

The merge runs in a single database transaction — it is all-or-nothing. If any conflict exists, execute is rejected until conflicts are resolved manually.

docs.title: Deleting a Branch
docs.text:
DELETE /api/graph/branches/{id}

Warning

Deleting a branch removes all objects that exist only on that branch. Objects that have been merged into the parent are unaffected.

docs.title: Renaming a Branch
docs.text:
PATCH /api/graph/branches/{id}
{ "name": "new-name" }

docs.title: Branch hierarchy
docs.text:
Branches can optionally record a parent_branch_id — which branch they were forked from. This is lineage metadata only and does not affect merge behavior. The merge compares object content hashes directly between source and target regardless of parentage.

A null parent_branch_id means the branch was created off the main graph.

main graph (no branch ID)
├── feature-a          (parent_branch_id: null)
│   └── feature-a-sub  (parent_branch_id: feature-a)
└── feature-b          (parent_branch_id: null)

Note

The main graph itself is not a branch and has no ID. To merge a branch into the main graph, you need the main graph's branch record ID — use GET /api/graph/branches to list all branches and identify the one representing main (typically the one with no parent and the earliest creation date).

docs.title: Letting an agent read unmerged branches
docs.text:
By default an agent searches the main graph only — pending work sitting on an unmerged branch is invisible to it. An agent definition can opt into reading branches that have not been merged yet, narrowed by why a branch exists and by its name:

PATCH /api/projects/{projectId}/agent-definitions/{id}
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "branchScope": {
    "unmerged": true,
    "origins": ["extraction"],
    "branches": ["extraction/*"],
    "maxBranches": 3
  }
}
Field Meaning unmerged true enables branch reads. Absent or false means main only. origins Only branches created by these sources: extraction, agent, manual, system. Empty/omitted allows any. branches Name globs. * is the only wildcard and it matches across /, so extraction/* covers every extraction branch. maxBranches How many branches one search may read, newest first. Default 3, maximum 20.

When both origins and branches are set, a branch must match both.

A search under a scope reads the main graph plus each matching branch and merges the results. Every object that exists only on a branch comes back flagged with branch_id, branch_name, origin and origin_label, so a model can say "on the pending extraction branch for Invoice.pdf…" rather than presenting it as settled fact. When the cap leaves branches unread, the response metadata carries a branch_scope_note saying so.

The boundary also follows the agent's calls: search-knowledge runs its internal research agent under the same boundary (it cannot be steered into reading a branch outside it), and a read tool that names a branch outside the boundary is refused.

It narrows reads; it grants nothing

A branch scope only restricts. No scope means main only: an agent that declares no branchScope reads the main graph, and a read tool that names a branch is refused — declaring a scope is what lets it read unmerged work. A scoped run may name only branches inside its scope, on any tool, so it cannot reach the rest by asking for one. Branch management is separate: an agent that could already create a branch and write to it still can (branch creation and writes are not gated by the read scope), and an agent allowed to merge a branch can always surface its content through main — that is a write-permission question, so grant write and merge rights on their own merits. A delegated sub-agent receives the intersection of its own scope and its caller's: a child can never read more than its parent, and a child that declares nothing of its own reads the main graph only.

Edge reads are bounded the same way: a scoped run sees relationships on the main graph and on the branches in its scope, and an agent run that declares no scope sees main edges only. Graph traversal is not widened by a scope yet — it walks the main graph — so a scoped agent reaches branch content through search, a branch named on a read tool, and search-knowledge.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: Chat lets you ask natural language questions about your knowledge graph and documents. The AI retrieves relevant context from your project and generates a grounded response with citations.

docs.title: Starting a Conversation
docs.text:
Admin UIAPI

Click Chat in the sidebar and start typing.

POST /api/chat/conversations
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "title": "Database architecture questions",
  "projectId": "proj_xyz789"
}

docs.title: Sending a Message
List conversations
docs.text: GET /api/chat/conversations

docs.title: Get a conversation with messages
docs.text: GET /api/chat/{id}

docs.title: Update a conversation
docs.text:
PATCH /api/chat/{id}
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "title": "Renamed conversation",
  "draftText": "Work in progress..."
}

docs.title: Delete a conversation
docs.text: DELETE /api/chat/{id}

docs.title: Conversation fields
docs.text: Field Description title Display name for the conversation isPrivate If true, only visible to you (default: true) enabledTools List of tool names the AI can use in this conversation agentDefinitionId Optional: link to a specific agent definition to use as the AI persona objectId / canonicalId Optional: pin the conversation to a specific graph object for focused Q&A

docs.title: Citations
docs.text:
Every assistant response includes citations — references to the graph objects or document chunks used to generate the answer. Citations appear in the citations field of the message:

{
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": "We decided to use PostgreSQL because of team expertise.",
  "citations": [
    {
      "type": "graph_object",
      "objectId": "<canonical_id>",
      "title": "Use PostgreSQL",
      "snippet": "Team expertise and existing infrastructure"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
The chat AI can call tools to answer questions. The available tools depend on what is enabled for the conversation:

Tool What it does graph_query Searches and retrieves graph objects search Runs hybrid search across documents and objects graph_create_object Creates a new graph object (write-enabled conversations)

Control which tools are available via enabledTools when creating or updating a conversation.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Be specific about type: "What Decision objects relate to authentication?" gives more precise results than "What do we know about auth?".
  • Reference objects by name: The AI can look up objects by their title or key property.
  • Long conversations: The platform maintains a context summary as conversations grow to keep responses relevant.

docs.title: Data Sources
docs.text: Data sources let you connect external systems to Memory and automatically import their content as documents. The platform periodically syncs new and updated content, keeping your knowledge graph current.

docs.title: Supported providers
docs.text:
Provider type Source type Description google_drive drive Google Drive files and folders gmail email Gmail threads github repo GitHub repositories (OAuth or a personal access token) trale meeting Trale meeting transcripts and summaries web web Web pages crawled from one or more start URLs

Google Drive and Gmail are OAuth-only

Both Google providers can only be connected via OAuth. There is no paste-a-refresh-token option. Data sources that were connected before this change with a stored refresh token keep syncing and do not need to be reconnected.

docs.title: Saved credentials
docs.text:
The Credentials page has two sections, each with its own heading. Saved credentials lists the project's reusable tokens; OAuth apps lists the vendor apps available to the project. The two are different things: a saved credential is a token you paste, an OAuth app is a client id/secret created in the vendor console — adding one never changes the other's status.

A saved credential is a token — today, a GitHub personal access token — stored once, encrypted, and reused by any number of data sources in the project. The list shows the name, the provider, how many sources use it, and when it was last changed; the token itself is never displayed again.

  • Add credential opens a dialog: choose the provider, name the credential, and paste the token. Only the fields that provider requires are asked for.
  • Edit reopens the same dialog with the name filled in. Renaming is safe, and leaving the token field empty keeps the stored token. Editing a credential changes it for every source that uses it, so a rotated token only needs to be updated once.
  • Reconnecting a source that uses a saved credential re-authorises the credential. The new grant replaces the stored token rather than being attached to that one source, so every enabled source using the credential resumes — including any that had parked as Needs reconnect, since a parked source is skipped by the scheduler and would otherwise never notice. A source you paused yourself stays paused: reconnecting repairs the credential, it does not override that decision. A credential that carries a token but no OAuth grant — a GitHub personal access token, say — is repaired by Reconnect as well, whenever the provider's OAuth client is available: consent replaces the stored token with an OAuth grant for the account that consents, for every source on the credential. To keep using the token instead, replace it by editing the credential, then set enabled: true on any of its sources that parked, because editing a credential does not change a source's status.
  • Delete is refused while a source still uses the credential; switch those sources to another credential first.

On a credentials connect form you can either select one of these saved credentials or create a new one without leaving the page — the new credential is selected for you when you return.

docs.title: Credentials (OAuth apps)
docs.text:
OAuth-based providers (Google Drive, GitHub) need an OAuth 2.0 app — a client that Memory uses to obtain access. Credentials are keyed by vendor, not by data source: one Google OAuth app can back Google Drive, and one GitHub OAuth app backs GitHub. The Data source column tells you which connection type the app backs.

The app can be configured at three levels, resolved in this order when a connection starts:

  1. Project — a project-level app, managed by a project_admin on the project's Settings → Credentials page. It overrides everything else for that project.
  2. Organization — an org-level app, managed by an org_admin under Organization Settings → Data source OAuth clients. That page is a table of providers, and each row opens that provider's editor — the same editor shape as the project page.
  3. Deployment default — a centrally configured app set via SOURCES_OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID / SOURCES_OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET (no setup needed by users).

If none is configured, connecting fails with an actionable message linking to the credentials page.

docs.title: The Credentials table
docs.text:
Project Settings → Credentials lists every OAuth-capable vendor as a table. Each provider has a project row, and gains an organization row only once an organization app is configured:

Column Meaning App The vendor-level app label, e.g. Google OAuth app Data source The connection type the app backs, e.g. Google Drive Scope Project or Organization Client ID The non-secret client id (secrets are never displayed) Status In use for the scope that wins resolution, Configured when it exists but is overridden, otherwise Not configured Updated When the app was last changed Actions Manage / Set up for admins; a role note for everyone else

A provider with no project and no organization app still shows its project row, so Set up stays reachable. The organization row appears only when that org app exists, which keeps the table one row per provider until someone configures the org scope. An admin's organization-row action opens the org's per-provider editor.

Every project member can view the table and see which app is in use. Only a project_admin can open the per-provider editor and change the project app; organization-wide apps are managed by org admins. Opening a per-provider editor as a non-admin returns 404.

docs.title: The organization OAuth apps table
docs.text:
Organization Settings → Data source OAuth clients lists each OAuth-capable provider as a row — app, data source, status, client id, updated — with a Set up or Manage action. That action opens /o/<org>/settings/oauth-clients/<provider>: the same OAuth-client card the project editor uses (client id, write-only secret, scopes, strategy, and the vendor console guide), with a back link to the table. Saving returns you to the table with a confirmation, and the stored secret is never shown again.

When no project or organization app exists and the deployment does not provide one, the page carries a note naming the providers that fall back to the deployment default.

The Data Sources page is a plain connections table (name, provider, status, sync mode, last sync) with a New data source action. It never asks you to configure credentials.

docs.title: Create the app in the vendor console
docs.text:
For Google Drive:

  1. Go to Google Cloud Console and create or select a project.
  2. Enable the Google Drive API.
  3. Configure the OAuth consent screen (External or Internal; for Workspace-internal apps use Internal).
  4. Under Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID, choose Web application.
  5. Under Authorized redirect URIs, add the Redirect URI shown on the credentials editor (it points at the Memory API callback, e.g. https://<api-host>/api/data-source-integrations/oauth/google_drive/callback).
  6. Under Authorized JavaScript origins, add the JavaScript origin shown on the same page (the Memory UI origin).
  7. Copy the Client ID and Client secret.
  8. Enable the Google Picker API for the same project.
  9. Create an API key (Credentials → Create credentials → API key) and restrict it to the Memory UI origin plus https://docs.google.com/*. Copy the key and the project number — they become the picker's Developer key and App ID in the credentials editor.

For Gmail, use the same Google Cloud project and OAuth client:

  1. Enable the Gmail API.
  2. Add the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly scope to the consent screen.
  3. Add the Gmail callback as an authorized redirect URI on the same web client: https://<api-host>/api/data-source-integrations/oauth/gmail/callback.

The Gmail scope is a Google restricted scope: an Internal (Workspace-only) consent screen can use it as-is, while an External app needs Google verification and a CASA assessment before non-test users can consent. See Gmail for the operational caveats.

A consent screen in Testing expires grants after 7 days — for Drive as well as Gmail

How long a connection lasts is decided by the publishing status of the OAuth client, not by the scope a source requested, so this applies to every Google source. While the app is in Testing, Google expires the authorization 7 days after consent, refresh token included: each source stops with its provider's message — "the Google Drive connection for this source has expired or was revoked", or the Gmail equivalent — parks as Needs reconnect, works again after reconnecting, and dies again a week later. Reconnecting cannot prevent it — the source is behaving correctly and reporting a grant that Google really did expire. Fix the client instead:

  • In production (or Internal for a Workspace) removes the 7-day clock, which is the only limit publishing status controls: the grant then lasts until it is revoked, or until another of Google's rules applies (six months unused, a password change on an account that granted Gmail scopes, the cap of 100 live refresh tokens per user per client). Publishing an Internal app needs no Google verification, though a Workspace administrator can still restrict which scopes the app is allowed to use.
  • An External app in production that uses drive.readonly or gmail.readonly needs Google's restricted-scope verification (and an annual security assessment), because both scopes give server-side access to user data. drive.file is not a restricted scope and takes the shorter review path.

Check Google Auth Platform → Audience: it shows the user type and publishing status of the project that owns the client. A client id pasted into a deployment inherits whatever that project says.

The picker keys are stored on the OAuth client that authorizes the source, so set them on the same project or organization client that holds the client id. A deployment-default client is environment configuration and has no editable config, so a source that resolves to it cannot load the picker until a project or organization client is configured.

docs.title: Enter the app
docs.text:
Project-levelOrganization-level

A project_admin opens Project Settings → Credentials, finds the Google OAuth app row, and chooses Manage (or Set up when it is not configured). The editor shows the Redirect URI and JavaScript origin to register in the vendor console, then takes the Client ID, Client secret, scopes, and strategy. This app is used only for that project.

An org_admin opens Organization Settings → Data source OAuth clients, chooses Google Drive, and enters the Client ID, Client secret, scopes, and strategy. This app is used for every project in the org that has not configured its own.

The Client secret is stored encrypted and is never shown again after saving — leave the secret field blank when updating other settings to keep the stored secret.

docs.title: Drive scope strategy
docs.text:
Google Drive has two selectable strategies, and they decide what the folder picker can see:

  • drive.readonly (default) — the app can list and read every file the connecting Google account can see, so the folder picker shows the whole drive. This is a restricted scope: a widely distributed app may need Google verification.
  • drive.file — the app sees only files it created or that a user picked through the Google Picker. That grant covers the picked object, not its children, so a drive.file source cannot browse or sync a folder tree. Folder sync needs drive.readonly; the source's detail page says so and links to Reconnect, which re-runs consent for that same source.

Whichever strategy you choose, the publishing status of the OAuth client decides how long a Drive connection lasts: an app left in Testing expires the grant 7 days after consent and the source parks as Needs reconnect until it is reconnected — see Create the app in the vendor console.

The strategy resolves project first, then organization, then the provider default. Leaving the project strategy blank inherits the organization's strategy; it does not reset to the default.

Changing the strategy applies to the next consent, not to sources that are already connected — a source keeps the scope its token was granted with. To move an existing source onto drive.readonly, switch the strategy and then press Reconnect on that source: consent runs again with the new scope and the source keeps its folders, cursor and history.

docs.title: Choosing folders in the Google Picker
docs.text:
A Drive source syncs the folders selected in the Google Picker. Open the source's detail page and press Choose folders (or follow the prompt on a freshly connected source):

  • The modal shows the folders the connected Google account can read. Open a folder to browse its subfolders; use the sidebar to switch between My Drive and Shared drives.
  • If Google asks you to sign in, use the account that connected this source. The Picker runs in your browser and needs a signed-in Google account — the token the server mints for the source is not enough on its own, and folders visible only to a different signed-in account are rejected when you save. Either pick again while signed in as the source's account, or share those folders with it; a folder shared with the source's account saves normally.
  • Select more than one folder. Selections accumulate across Picker openings, so you can add a folder, close the picker, browse elsewhere, and add another.
  • Remove a folder with the × on its chip, then press Save folders.

Each picked folder is stored as {folder_id, name, drive_id}. name and drive_id are resolved from Drive when you save, so a renamed or moved folder stays identifiable. One source accepts at most 50 folders; mime_types and recursive apply to all of them. A file that appears in two selected folders is ingested once per sync.

Subfolder inclusion still follows the Recursive setting: recursive sync walks below each selected folder, non-recursive sync ingests the folder's direct children only.

The source detail page also shows the credentials in use: the OAuth app scope (project, organization, or deployment default), the short client id, the connected Google account, and the granted scope. Manage credentials opens Settings → Credentials.

Free-text folder ids from older clients are still accepted: the first update rewrites folder_id/shared_drive_id into the canonical folders list.

GitHub accepts either an OAuth app (the same project/organization resolution) or a personal access token entered when connecting the source; a token connection does not need an OAuth app.

docs.title: Gmail (email)
docs.text:
Select Gmail on Data Sources → New data source and authorize with the Google account whose mail you want to sync.
